'''''Rudbeckia fulgida''''', the '''orange coneflower'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=RUFU2|taxon=Rudbeckia fulgida|accessdate=25 October 2015}}</ref> or '''perennial coneflower''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] Asteraceae, [[native plant|native]] to eastern North America.

==Description==
It is an [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] growing up to {{convert|120|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall, with bright yellow daisy-like [[pseudanthium|composite]] flower heads.{{cn|date=September 2024}}

===Growth and reproduction===
''Rudbeckia fulgida'' spreads by both [[stolon]]iferous stems and seed. The seeds are produced in fruits called cypselae, which are {{convert|2.2|to|4|mm|2}} long and have short coroniform [[Pappus (flower structure)|pappi]] {{convert|0.2|mm|3}} long.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242417172 |title=Rudbeckia fulgida |department=Flora of North America |website=efloras.org}}</ref>

The ripe seed is a favorite food of finches in winter.{{cn|date=September 2024}}

===Morphology===
{{cn span|Stems are hairy, ridged, and dark green. Leaves are dark green, sparsely but roughly haired, simple, with sparsely serrate margins. [[Flower]]s are heads, with black disk florets and bright orange ray florets, borne singly on stems that extend above the foliage. Stems are glabrous (smooth) or moderately hirsute (hairy) with spreading branches. The leaves have blades that are lanceolate to broadly ovate or elliptic in shape without lobes. The leaf bases are attenuate to cordate in shape and the margins of the leaves are usually entire or serrate, or sometimes lacerate. The upper surfaces of the leaves are glabrous or have hirsute to strigose hairs. The basal leaves are petiolate, with petioles that are {{convert|5|–|30|cm|0}} long  and {{convert|1|–|8|cm|1}} wide, the cauline or stem leaves have petioles that are {{convert|2|–|25|cm|1}} long and {{convert|0.5|–|7|cm|1}} wide, the bases are attenuate to cordate or auriculate in shape.|date=September 2024}}

{{cn span|The flower heads are often produced one per stem but are also often produced in corymbiform arrays with 2 to 7 flowers per stem. The cups that hold the flowers called receptacles, are hemispheric to ovoid in shape with [[paleae]] {{convert|2.5|–|4|mm|2}} long, the apices are obtuse to acute in shape with the ends usually glabrous and the apical margins ciliate. The flower heads have 10 to 15 ray florets with laminae elliptic to oblanceolate in shape and {{convert|15|–|25|cm}} long and {{convert|3|–|6|mm}} wide. The abaxially surfaces of the laminae have strigose hairs. The flower discs or center cones are {{convert|12|–|16|mm}} tall and {{convert|10|–|18|mm}} wide, made up of 50 to over 500 disc florets, with the corollas proximally yellowish green and brown-purple distally in color, {{convert|3|–|4.2|mm}} long, having style branches {{convert|1.3|mm|2}} long.|date=September 2024}}

== Ecology ==

=== Habitat ===
''R. fulgida'' may be found in a variety of habitats such as bogs, woodlands, bottomlands, and [[calcareous]] slopes.<ref>Weakley, A. S. (2015). ''Flora of the Southern and Mid-Atlantic States''. Chapel Hill, NC, University of North Carolina Herbarium.</ref> 

=== Phenology ===
This species has been observed to flower from January through September.<ref>Nelson, G. PanFlora: Plant data for the eastern United States with emphasis on the Southeastern Coastal Plains, Florida, and the Florida Panhandle. www.gilnelson.com/PanFlora/ Accessed: 29 MAY 2018.</ref>

==Etymology==
The Latin [[specific epithet]] ''fulgida'' means "shining" or "glistening".<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book | last = Harrison | first = Lorraine | title = RHS Latin for Gardeners | year=2012 |publisher = Mitchell Beazley | location = United Kingdom | isbn = 978-1845337315}}</ref>

The plant is a source of [[fulgidic acid]] named after it.

==Cultivation==
There are seven varieties;
* ''Rudbeckia fulgida'' var. ''deamii'' <small>([[Sidney Fay Blake|S. F. Blake]]) Perdue</small> - Deam's coneflower
* ''Rudbeckia fulgida'' var. ''fulgida'' <small>[[William Aiton|Aiton]]</small> - orange coneflower
* ''Rudbeckia fulgida'' var. ''palustris'' <small>(Eggert ex C.L. Boynt. & Beadle) Perdue</small> - orange coneflower, prairie coneflower
* ''Rudbeckia fulgida'' var. ''spathulata'' <small>([[André Michaux|Michx.]]) Perdue</small> - orange coneflower
* ''Rudbeckia fulgida'' var. ''speciosa'' <small>([[Georg Wilhelm Franz Wenderoth|Wender.]]) Perdue</small> - orange coneflower
* ''Rudbeckia fulgida'' var. ''sullivantii'' <small>(C.L. Boynt. & Beadle) [[Arthur Cronquist|Cronquist]]</small> - Sullivant's coneflower
* ''Rudbeckia fulgida'' var. ''umbrosa'' <small>(C.L. Boynt. & Beadle) [[Arthur Cronquist|Cronquist]]</small> - orange coneflower
<ref>[https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=36770 ITIS Report: Rudbeckia fulgida  Aiton]</ref>

''Rudbeckia fulgida'' var. ''deamii''<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Rudbeckia fulgida'' var. 'deamii'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/58880/Rudbeckia-fulgida-var-deamii/Details | access-date = 17 February 2021}}</ref> and ''R. fulgida'' var. * 'Pot of Gold' - 10 weeks at {{convert|35|-|41|°F}} <ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.gpnmag.com/article/rudbeckia-fulgida-pot-gold/|title=Rudbeckia fulgida 'Pot Of Gold' – Greenhouse Product News|website=www.gpnmag.com|access-date=2016-12-27}}</ref>
